content.text: The Solar System is our cosmic neighbourhood. It consists of a central star, the Sun, along with all the objects that are gravitationally bound to it: eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and vast quantities of dust and gas. Understanding the Solar System is fundamental to understanding our place in the universe and the physical laws that govern the motion of celestial bodies.

Humans have studied the night sky for thousands of years, but it is only in the last few centuries that we have developed a scientific understanding of how the Solar System is structured and why objects move the way they do. The key to this understanding is gravity, the universal force of attraction between all objects that have mass.
In this lesson, we will explore the structure of the Solar System, the characteristics of its major components, and the role that gravity plays in keeping everything in its place.

The Sun is a medium-sized star located at the centre of the Solar System. It is a massive sphere of hot gas (mostly hydrogen and helium) that produces energy through nuclear fusion. In its core, hydrogen nuclei fuse together to form helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy in the process. This energy is radiated outward as light and heat, providing the warmth and illumination that make life on Earth possible.

The Sun contains about 99.86% of the total mass of the entire Solar System. This enormous mass is what creates the gravitational field that holds all the planets, moons, and other objects in orbit.
The Solar System contains eight planets, which are divided into two groups: the inner rocky planets (also called terrestrial planets) and the outer gas and ice giants.
is the closest planet to the Sun, orbiting at an average distance of about 0.39 AU (where 1 AU, or astronomical unit, is the average distance from the Earth to the Sun, approximately

m). Mercury is the smallest planet in the Solar System, with a diameter of about 4,880 km. It has virtually no atmosphere, which means its surface experiences extreme temperature variations: up to 430 degrees Celsius on the sunlit side and as low as -180 degrees Celsius on the dark side. Mercury has no moons and completes one orbit around the Sun in about 88 Earth days.

is the second planet from the Sun, orbiting at about 0.72 AU. Venus is sometimes called Earth's "twin" because it is similar in size and mass to Earth (diameter about 12,100 km). However, its conditions are drastically different. Venus has an extremely thick atmosphere composed mainly of carbon dioxide, which creates a runaway greenhouse effect. This makes Venus the hottest planet in the Solar System, with surface temperatures reaching about 470 degrees Celsius, even hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. Venus has no moons and its orbital period is about 225 Earth days. Unusually, Venus rotates on its axis in the opposite direction to most other planets (retrograde rotation).

is the third planet from the Sun, orbiting at 1.00 AU. Earth has a diameter of about 12,742 km and is the only planet known to support life. Earth has a nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere, liquid water on its surface, and a magnetic field that protects it from harmful solar radiation. Earth has one natural satellite, the Moon, and completes one orbit around the Sun in approximately 365.25 days.

is the fourth planet from the Sun, orbiting at about 1.52 AU. Mars is often called the "Red Planet" because of its reddish appearance, caused by iron oxide (rust) on its surface. Mars is smaller than Earth, with a diameter of about 6,790 km. It has a thin atmosphere composed mostly of carbon dioxide, and surface temperatures range from about -140 degrees Celsius to 20 degrees Celsius. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, and its orbital period is about 687 Earth days. Mars is currently a major target for space exploration, with several robotic missions studying its surface and atmosphere.
The Outer Planets (Gas and Ice Giants)

is the fifth planet from the Sun, orbiting at about 5.20 AU. Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System, with a diameter of about 139,800 km (more than 11 times that of Earth). It is a gas giant composed mainly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface. Jupiter is famous for its Great Red Spot, a massive storm that has been raging for hundreds of years. Jupiter has at least 95 known moons, including the four large Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. Its orbital period is about 11.9 Earth years.

is the sixth planet from the Sun, orbiting at about 9.54 AU. Saturn is the second-largest planet, with a diameter of about 116,500 km. Like Jupiter, it is a gas giant composed primarily of hydrogen and helium. Saturn is best known for its spectacular ring system, which is made up of billions of particles of ice and rock ranging in size from tiny grains to large boulders. Saturn has over 140 known moons, including Titan, which has a thick atmosphere and liquid methane lakes on its surface. Saturn's orbital period is about 29.5 Earth years.

is the seventh planet from the Sun, orbiting at about 19.2 AU. Uranus is an ice giant with a diameter of about 50,700 km. Its atmosphere contains hydrogen, helium, and methane, and it is the methane that gives Uranus its distinctive blue-green colour. Uranus is unique in that it rotates on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees. Uranus has 27 known moons and a faint ring system. Its orbital period is about 84 Earth years.

is the eighth and most distant planet from the Sun, orbiting at about 30.1 AU. Neptune is an ice giant similar in size to Uranus, with a diameter of about 49,500 km. Like Uranus, it has a blue colour due to methane in its atmosphere. Neptune has the strongest winds of any planet in the Solar System, reaching speeds of over 2,000 km/h. Neptune has 16 known moons, the largest being Triton, and a faint ring system. Its orbital period is about 165 Earth years.

A dwarf planet is an object that orbits the Sun, has enough mass for gravity to pull it into a roughly spherical shape, but has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit of other debris. The most famous dwarf planet is

, which was reclassified from a planet to a dwarf planet in 2006. Pluto orbits at an average distance of about 39.5 AU and has five known moons, the largest being Charon. Other dwarf planets include Eris, Ceres (located in the asteroid belt), Makemake, and Haumea.

A moon, or natural satellite, is an object that orbits a planet or dwarf planet rather than the Sun directly. Moons are held in orbit by the gravitational attraction of their parent body. The Solar System contains hundreds of known moons. Earth's Moon is our most familiar natural satellite, with a diameter of about 3,474 km. It orbits the Earth at an average distance of about 384,400 km and plays a significant role in causing tides on Earth through its gravitational pull.

Some moons are particularly interesting from a scientific perspective. Europa (a moon of Jupiter) is thought to have a liquid water ocean beneath its icy surface, making it a candidate for harbouring life. Titan (a moon of Saturn) has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane.
Asteroids are rocky and metallic objects that orbit the Sun but are too small to be classified as planets or dwarf planets. Most asteroids are found in the

, a region of space located between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, roughly 2.1 to 3.3 AU from the Sun. The asteroid belt contains millions of asteroids, ranging in size from tiny pebbles to objects hundreds of kilometres across. The largest object in the asteroid belt is the dwarf planet Ceres, which has a diameter of about 940 km.
Asteroids are thought to be remnants from the early Solar System that never formed into a planet, largely due to the gravitational influence of Jupiter disrupting their orbits.

Comets are small icy bodies that orbit the Sun, typically in highly elliptical (elongated) orbits. A comet is composed of a mixture of ice (water ice, carbon dioxide ice, methane ice), dust, and rocky material. This composition has led to comets being described as "dirty snowballs."

When a comet's orbit brings it close to the Sun, the heat causes the ice to sublimate (turn directly from solid to gas), releasing gas and dust. This creates a glowing cloud around the comet's nucleus called the
, and the solar wind and radiation pressure push this material outward to form one or two
: a dust tail (which curves gently along the orbit) and an ion tail (which points directly away from the Sun). Comets can have tails stretching millions of kilometres into space.
Comets originate from two main regions:
, a region of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune (about 30 to 50 AU from the Sun), which is the source of short-period comets.
, a hypothetical spherical shell of icy objects extending from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU from the Sun, which is the source of long-period comets.
Famous comets include Halley's Comet, which has an orbital period of about 76 years and last appeared in 1986.
The Scale of the Solar System and the Astronomical Unit
The Solar System is incredibly vast. To make the enormous distances more manageable, astronomers use the
, defined as the average distance from the Earth to the Sun:

Using this unit, the distances to the planets become easier to compare. For example, Mercury orbits at about 0.39 AU, while Neptune orbits at about 30.1 AU. This means Neptune is roughly 77 times farther from the Sun than Mercury.

To appreciate the scale, if the Sun were reduced to the size of a basketball (about 24 cm in diameter), the Earth would be a small bead about 2 mm in diameter located about 26 metres away, and Neptune would be about 780 metres away.
All objects with mass attract each other through the force of gravity. The gravitational force between two objects depends on their masses and the distance between them.
The greater the masses, the stronger the gravitational force.
The Sun's enormous mass creates a very strong gravitational field that extends throughout the Solar System.
The greater the distance, the weaker the gravitational force.
Gravity follows an inverse square law: if you double the distance, the force decreases to one quarter of its original value.

A planet in orbit around the Sun is continuously falling towards the Sun due to gravitational attraction. However, the planet also has a velocity directed sideways (tangentially to its orbit). The combination of the inward gravitational pull and the sideways motion results in a curved path: an orbit.
The gravitational force acts as a

, constantly pulling the planet towards the centre of its orbit (the Sun) and changing the direction of the planet's velocity. Without gravity, the planet would fly off in a straight line. Without its sideways velocity, the planet would fall directly into the Sun.

Planets closer to the Sun orbit faster, and planets farther from the Sun orbit slower. For example, Mercury (the closest planet) has an orbital speed of about 47.4 km/s, while Neptune (the most distant planet) has an orbital speed of only about 5.4 km/s.

is the time it takes for a planet to complete one full orbit around the Sun. The orbital period increases with orbital radius. Planets farther from the Sun take longer to complete one orbit, both because they travel more slowly and because they have a larger orbit to traverse.

Misconception 1: "The asteroid belt is densely packed with rocks"

In films and television, the asteroid belt is often depicted as a dangerous region where spacecraft must dodge rocks at every turn. In reality, the asteroid belt is mostly empty space. The average distance between asteroids is millions of kilometres, and spacecraft have passed through the belt many times without any difficulty.
Misconception 2: "Planets orbit because they are being pushed outward by centrifugal force"

There is no outward force acting on an orbiting planet. The only force is gravity, pulling the planet inward towards the Sun. The planet does not fly away because its sideways velocity constantly carries it past the Sun. The so-called "centrifugal force" is not a real force; it is an effect experienced in a rotating reference frame.

The Sun does not burn through combustion (a chemical reaction with oxygen). Instead, it produces energy through nuclear fusion, where hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium under extreme temperature and pressure conditions. This is a nuclear process, not a chemical one, and produces vastly more energy than any fire could.
Misconception 4: "Pluto was demoted because it is small"

Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet not simply because of its size, but because it has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. There are many other objects of comparable size in similar orbits in the Kuiper Belt. The definition of a planet requires that the object has cleared its orbital path of other debris.
Misconception 5: "All planets orbit in perfect circles"

While many planetary orbits are close to circular, they are actually ellipses (slightly stretched circles). Some objects, like comets, have highly elliptical orbits that take them very close to the Sun and then far away.

The Solar System consists of the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, and comets, all held together by gravity.
The Sun is a star that produces energy through nuclear fusion and contains about 99.86% of the Solar System's mass.
The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small, rocky terrestrial planets. The four outer planets include two gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) and two ice giants (Uranus, Neptune).
Dwarf planets, such as Pluto, orbit the Sun but have not cleared their orbital neighbourhood.
Asteroids are rocky objects mostly found in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy bodies with highly elliptical orbits that develop tails when they approach the Sun.
Gravity is the force that keeps planets and other objects in orbit around the Sun. The gravitational force follows an inverse square law: doubling the distance reduces the force to one quarter.

Venus has an extremely thick atmosphere composed mainly of carbon dioxide. This creates a runaway greenhouse effect, trapping heat radiated from the planet's surface. Mercury has virtually no atmosphere, so it cannot retain heat. The greenhouse effect on Venus raises its surface temperature to about 470 degrees Celsius, making it hotter than Mercury despite receiving less solar radiation.

A comet is composed of a mixture of ice (water ice, carbon dioxide ice, methane ice), dust, and rocky material. It has a solid nucleus surrounded by these materials. As it approaches the Sun, the increased heat causes the ice to sublimate (change directly from solid to gas), releasing gas and dust. This forms a glowing cloud called the coma around the nucleus. The solar wind and radiation pressure push this material outward to form one or two tails: a curved dust tail and a straight ion tail pointing directly away from the Sun.

Mercury orbits faster than Neptune. Mercury has an orbital speed of about 47.4 km/s, while Neptune orbits at only about 5.4 km/s. This is because planets closer to the Sun experience a stronger gravitational pull, requiring a higher orbital speed to maintain a stable orbit. Kepler's Third Law (
) confirms that closer planets have shorter periods and therefore higher speeds.
Asteroids are composed of rock and metal, while comets are composed of ice, dust, and rocky material.

Asteroids are mostly found in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, while comets originate from the Kuiper Belt or the Oort Cloud and typically have highly elliptical orbits that bring them close to the Sun.
